gap_note: None of the three domains that rank for this term — us.ovhcloud.com, digitalocean.com, lowendbox.com — serves a downloadable price-comparison file in their top pages. This page hands you the file and keeps it in sync with the tracked plans.
answer: Download unit-price.csv: every tracked plan with a published price, plus the RAM and vCPU figures that were published next to it, and a computed price per GB of RAM and per vCPU.
body_html:
The file

Download unit-price.csv

The CSV is written by the same build that renders this page, so it always matches the price table on the site. Columns: provider, plan, price, currency, ram_gb, vcpu, disk_gb, price_per_gb_ram, price_per_vcpu, unit_price_formula, source_url, fetched_at.

What is in it and what is not

A row carries a per-GB number only when the provider published a RAM figure in the same place as the price. Rows without a published RAM figure keep that cell empty on purpose: a headline price on its own cannot be converted into a per-GB figure without inventing the denominator.

How to recompute any row yourself

Every per-unit cell equals price ÷ ram_gb (or price ÷ vcpu). The unit_price_formula column spells out the arithmetic for the row, and source_url plus fetched_at say which public page it was read from and when.

title: How to pick a cheap VPS plan, deploy it, and connect (numbered steps)
gap_note: The top pages for this term in the three benchmarked domains describe plans but do not walk you through the purchase-to-login sequence. The steps below are taken from provider-published documentation, with the source linked at each step.
answer: Pick by RAM per dollar and published bandwidth, deploy from the provider panel, then connect over SSH (Linux) or RDP (Windows). The whole sequence is eight steps below.
body_html:
1. Decide the resource floor from the workload, not from the price. Write down the smallest RAM figure that will run your stack. A single small web app or VPN fits in 1–2 GB; a database doing real work wants 4 GB or more.
  2. Compare plans on published numbers only. Use the CSV and divide price by the RAM figure the provider published. If a plan publishes no RAM figure next to the price, treat the per-GB number as unknown rather than guessing it.
  3. Check what the price excludes before you commit. Backups, control panels, extra IPv4 addresses and Windows licences are commonly billed separately. Open the provider's pricing page and read the row under the plan card.
  4. Create the account and deploy the server. From the provider's control panel choose the plan, the data-centre region closest to your users, and the operating system image. Linux distributions are offered at no extra licence cost on the low-cost plans; Windows normally adds a licence fee.
  5. Whitelist your SSH key. Paste your public key during deployment. With key authentication you can disable password login later instead of relying on a password over the open internet.
  6. Connect over SSH (Linux plans). The provider gives you the server's IPv4 address at deploy time; connect from a terminal with the username and key you configured. An out-of-band console in the panel is the fallback when SSH does not answer.
  7. Connect over RDP (Windows plans). A Windows VPS is reached with Remote Desktop to the server address using the administrator credentials the provider issued. If the vendor documents a bring-your-own-licence path, activate your own retail or volume licence after installation.
  8. Update, then harden before you point traffic at it. Apply operating-system updates, replace password login with keys where the OS supports it, open only the ports you need, and confirm you have a backup or snapshot you can actually restore.

What this sequence does not include

Control-panel installation, application deployment and migration are separate tasks; providers document those on their own help pages, and this page does not paraphrase them.

title: How VPS pricing actually works: per-GB RAM, egress and the licence that is not in the headline price
gap_note: The benchmarked pages list plan prices but do not break them down per unit. This page computes the per-unit figure from published prices only, and is explicit about which plans cannot be computed at all.
answer: Rank plans by price divided by published RAM in GB. Where RAM is not published next to the price, the per-GB figure is unknown — a headline price alone cannot rank two plans.
body_html:
Why the headline price cannot rank plans

Two plans at the same monthly price are not the same product. One may include twice the memory of the other, or include it in a different currency, or leave the memory figure off the pricing page altogether. Dividing the published price by the published RAM figure is the only comparison that needs no assumption.

The three inputs a per-GB number needs

  1. The plan's monthly price, exactly as published.
  2. The RAM figure for that same plan, from the same page.
  3. Which page and which read time the two came from.

If any of the three is missing, the per-GB number is unknown. This site leaves the cell empty in that case; it does not estimate.

What this site does not do

It does not convert currencies, because a converted number is no longer the number the provider published. It does not treat a promotional first-month price as the ongoing price. It does not compare a plan's price against another plan's specification.

How to recompute every cell

Each unit price is the published monthly price divided by the figure the provider printed beside it (1 TB = 1000 GB). Currencies are grouped and never converted at an exchange rate we cannot verify. A plan that publishes no figure gets no row instead of an estimate.
